newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis equals Latin American siege record.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis equals Latin American siege record.

text.p: Peru's standoff with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages entered its 61st day on Sunday, equalling the previous longest hostage siege in Latin America's turbulent 20th-century guerrilla history.

In a strikingly similar drama, a 15-strong commando unit of Colombian M-19 guerrillas held 57 hostages -- including 19 diplomats -- at the Dominican Embassy in Bogota for 61 days in 1980 before releasing them and taking refuge in Cuba.
Peru's rebel hostage-takers also number about 15, hold some diplomats among their 72 hostages, and have been offered asylum abroad. But an end to the Lima crisis on its 61st day is unlikely.
Rather, the saga has returned to a familiar daily routine after three rounds of talks brought frenetic activity at the siege site but little tangible progress.
Police resumed their psychological tactics against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, playing traditional "criollo" music for several hours in the morning.
They also sent a helicopter flying low over the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, the Vatican's representative on a peace commission overseeing talks between the government and rebels, returned to the residence on Sunday to give the hostages their weekly mass. He made no comments on entering the building.

Several hundred people waving balloons and placards joined a Rotary Club-organised "March for Peace" outside the residence -- the latest in the near-daily series of demonstrations and rallies at the site.
Taking advantage of the hordes of journalists still staking out the diplomatic compound, a small commercial plane trailing an advertisement for a local bank flew over the site twice.
The only unusual activity was the detention in the early hours of a local cameraman who strayed beyond security lines and was taken away for questioning by anti-terrorism police.
Sunday's activity followed talks on three previous days at a safe house opposite the residence between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA No. 2 Rolly Rojas.

A Red Cross car transported Rojas on each occasion into the house, where a metal detector was used to ensure nobody entered with weapons, and cables were laid to apparently provide a phone link with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, one of three members of a guarantors' committee overseeing the talks, said the only agreement so far between the two sides was to allow the mediators to "elaborate a proposal that will facilitate the continuation of the preliminary conversations."

Normally pro-government daily Expreso summed up the mood of pessimism among local media with a headline describing the new talks as a "dialogue between deaf people." It blamed rebel "intransigence" for the apparent lack of progress.

The renewal of dialogue last Tuesday at least broke weeks of deadlock since first face-to-face talks Dec. 28 later stalled on the rebels' demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades. The government has refused to consider this issue.

The band of heavily-armed, Cuban-inspired rebels initially took more than 500 hostages after storming the residence during a Dec. 17 cocktail party. But it has since released all but 72 captives, including Fujimori's brother, two cabinet ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
